claim: RRF depletion leads to enrichment of post-termination 70S complexes in 3′-UTRs.
source: As expected, RRF depletion leads to enrichment of post-termination 70S complexes in 3′-UTRs.
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data showing accumulation of ribosome density in 3′-UTRs upon RRF depletion (Figure 2).

claim: Elongating ribosomes are unable to complete translation because they are blocked by non-recycled ribosomes at stop codons when RRF is depleted.
source: We also observe that elongating ribosomes are unable to complete translation because they are blocked by non-recycled ribosomes at stop codons.
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data showing stacked ribosomes upstream of stop codons (Figure 2).

claim: RRF depletion did not significantly affect coupling efficiency in reporter assays.
source: We found, however, that RRF depletion did not significantly affect coupling efficiency in reporter assays or in ribosome density genome-wide.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assays showing no significant change in coupling efficiency upon RRF depletion (Figure 5).

claim: RRF depletion did not significantly affect coupling efficiency in ribosome density genome-wide.
source: We found, however, that RRF depletion did not significantly affect coupling efficiency in reporter assays or in ribosome density genome-wide.
evidence: Supported by genome-wide ribosome profiling analysis showing high correlation of upstream/downstream gene ratios between WT and RRF KD strains (Figure 6).

claim: Re-initiation is not a major mechanism of translational coupling in E. coli.
source: These findings argue that re-initiation is not a major mechanism of translational coupling in E. coli.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of RRF depletion on translational coupling efficiency.

claim: RRF depletion has dramatic effects on the activity of ribosome rescue factors tmRNA and ArfA.
source: Finally, RRF depletion has dramatic effects on the activity of ribosome rescue factors tmRNA and ArfA.
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling and RNA-seq data showing increased ribosome footprints on tmRNA and 39-fold upregulation of ArfA (Figure 7).

claim: In eukaryotes and archaea, termination is carried out by a complex containing both a release factor and a translational GTPase.
source: These differences are already evident in the termination step: in eukaryotes and archaea, termination is carried out by a complex containing both a release factor and a translational GTPase (eRF1 and eRF3 in eukaryotes) (Frolova et al., 1994; Alkalaeva et al., 2006; Saito et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: eRF1 remains in the ribosome after the release of the nascent peptide and helps recruit the factor that catalyzes subunit splitting.
source: eRF1 remains in the ribosome after the release of the nascent peptide and helps recruit the factor that catalyzes subunit splitting, Rli1 (in yeast) or ABCE1 (in mammals) (Pisarev et al., 2010; Shoemaker and Green, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Bacterial release factors RF1 and RF2 are evolutionarily unrelated to eukaryotic release factors and act alone to release the nascent peptide.
source: In contrast, although the bacterial release factors RF1 and RF2 share similar names with their eukaryotic counterparts, they are evolutionarily unrelated and act alone to release the nascent peptide (Scolnick et al., 1968).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: RRF works together with the GTPase EFG to promote subunit splitting and release of the large subunit in bacteria.
source: In a mechanism unique to bacteria, RRF works together with the GTPase EFG to promote subunit splitting and release of the large subunit (Janosi et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Binding of IF3 excludes the deacylated tRNA from the 30S subunit and prevents reassembly of the 70S complex.
source: Binding of IF3 then excludes the deacylated tRNA from the 30S subunit and prevents reassembly of the 70S complex (Prabhakar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Depletion of Rli1 in S. cerevisiae results in an accumulation of ribosome density at stop codons and a queue of elongating ribosomes that collide with post-TCs at defined distances upstream of stop codons.
source: Recent studies in Saccharomyces cerevisiae using ribosome profiling to study recycling factors in vivo revealed that depletion of the 80S recycling factor Rli1 results in an accumulation of ribosome density at stop codons, consistent with a build-up of post-TCs that fail to be recycled, and an associated queue of elongating ribosomes that collide with these post-TCs at defined distances upstream of stop codons (Young et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Rli1 knockdown in S. cerevisiae results in abundant ribosome density in the 3′-UTR, some of which can be attributed to translating ribosomes that re-initiated downstream of the stop codon.
source: These studies also reported abundant ribosome density in the 3′-UTR upon Rli1 knockdown. Some of this density can be attributed to translating ribosomes that re-initiated downstream of the stop codon, although the mechanism of this re-initiation is yet to be elucidated.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Depletion of 40S recycling factors Tma64/Tma22/Tma20 in S. cerevisiae results in stacked ribosomes upstream of the stop codon and re-initiation arising from 40S scanning ribosomes in the 3′-UTR.
source: In a later study, Guydosh and co-workers depleted the 40S recycling factors Tma64/Tma22/Tma20, again observing stacked ribosomes upstream of the stop codon and re-initiation arising from 40S scanning ribosomes in the 3′-UTR (Young et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The direct consequence of loss of recycling in yeast is unintended re-initiation in untranslated regions.
source: These reports validate previous biochemical work on these ribosome recycling factors in yeast and reveal that the direct consequence of loss of recycling is unintended re-initiation in untranslated regions.
evidence: Inferred from studies on yeast recycling factors cited in the text.

claim: Genes encoded in the same mRNA are said to be translationally coupled when the translation of the upstream gene promotes translation of the downstream gene.
source: Genes encoded in the same mRNA are said to be translationally coupled when the translation of the upstream gene promotes translation of the downstream gene.
evidence: This is a definition based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Coupling was first reported in genetic studies in which nonsense mutations in an upstream gene suppress translation of a downstream gene.
source: Coupling was first reported in genetic studies in which nonsense mutations in an upstream gene suppress translation of a downstream gene (Oppenheim and Yanofsky, 1980).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Translational coupling is a conserved mechanism observed in a number of genes across various bacterial species and their phages.
source: Such translational coupling is a conserved mechanism, observed in a number of genes across various bacterial species and their phages (Berkhout and van Duin, 1985; van de Guchte et al., 1991; Govantes et al., 1998; Grabowska et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Distances less than 25 nt between the stop codon of the upstream gene and the start codon of the downstream gene are optimal for coupling to occur.
source: One of the key features regulating coupling efficiency is the distance between the stop codon of the upstream gene and the start codon of the downstream gene: distances less than 25 nt are optimal for coupling to occur (Levin-Karp et al., 2013; Tian and Salis, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 75% of intergenic regions in polycistronic transcripts are shorter than 25 nt in Escherichia coli.
source: 75% of intergenic regions in polycistronic transcripts are shorter than this distance in Escherichia coli (Yamamoto et al., 2016), indicating that a high percentage of genes are optimally positioned for translational coupling.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A high percentage of genes in E. coli are optimally positioned for translational coupling.
source: 75% of intergenic regions in polycistronic transcripts are shorter than this distance in Escherichia coli (Yamamoto et al., 2016), indicating that a high percentage of genes are optimally positioned for translational coupling.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that 75% of intergenic regions are shorter than the optimal distance for coupling.

claim: One proposed mechanism of translational coupling is that ribosomes translating the upstream gene may unwind secondary structures that otherwise block de novo initiation at the downstream gene.
source: Two main mechanisms have been proposed in the literature: (1) ribosomes translating the upstream gene may unwind secondary structures that otherwise block de novo initiation at the downstream gene (Baughman and Nomura, 1983)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: One proposed mechanism of translational coupling is that following termination and subunit splitting by RRF, 30S subunits may scan along the mRNA and re-initiate on the downstream gene without dissociating from the message.
source: or (2) following termination at the upstream stop codon and subunit splitting by RRF, 30S subunits may scan along the mRNA and re-initiate on the downstream gene without dissociating from the message (Adhin and van Duin, 1990; Rex et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A model involving re-initiation by 70S post-TCs has been proposed for translational coupling.
source: More recently, a model involving re-initiation by 70S post-TCs has also been proposed (Yamamoto et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Using a temperature-sensitive RRF allele, Kaji and co-workers reported higher levels of downstream gene expression on reporter constructs when RRF activity is reduced.
source: Using a temperature-sensitive RRF allele, Kaji and co-workers reported higher levels of downstream gene expression on reporter constructs when RRF activity is reduced (Janosi et al., 1998), consistent with models of re-initiation by post-TCs.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Analysis of several coupled phage genes revealed no evidence that coupling depends on ribosome recycling.
source: In contrast, using similar approaches, analysis of several coupled phage genes revealed no evidence that coupling depends on ribosome recycling (Inokuchi et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Nakamura and co-workers studied re-initiation after premature stop codons within the phoA gene in E. coli and argued against a role for RRF.
source: Using a different strategy to deplete RRF (transcriptional shut-off with a ligand-inducible promoter), Nakamura and co-workers studied re-initiation after premature stop codons (i.e. nonsense mutations) within the phoA gene in E. coli and also argued against a role for RRF (Karamyshev et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The promoter upstream of frr (the gene encoding RRF) was replaced by the ligand-inducible araBAD promoter in the genome.
source: To accomplish this, we swapped the promoter in the genome with the araBAD promoter so that cells cultured in media with arabinose express RRF, but following the switch to media with glucose, they strongly repress its transcription.
evidence: Described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A FLAG-epitope was added to the C-terminus of RRF to facilitate its detection.
source: In addition, we added a FLAG-epitope to the C-terminus of RRF to facilitate its detection, and the short peptide tag YALAA to target the protein for degradation by ClpXP (Carr et al., 2012).
evidence: Described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The short peptide tag YALAA was added to RRF to target the protein for degradation by ClpXP.
source: In addition, we added a FLAG-epitope to the C-terminus of RRF to facilitate its detection, and the short peptide tag YALAA to target the protein for degradation by ClpXP (Carr et al., 2012).
evidence: Described in the text and shown in Figure 1A, with citation to prior research on ClpXP degradation.

claim: 10 min after the media switch to glucose, RRF levels are visibly reduced in immunoblots.
source: In media containing glucose, the combination of transcriptional shut-off and accelerated protein degradation yield rapid depletion of the RRF protein: 10 min after the media switch, RRF levels are visibly reduced in immunoblots; 15 min following a second transfer to fresh media containing glucose, the protein is nearly undetectable (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 15 min following a second transfer to fresh media containing glucose, RRF protein is nearly undetectable.
source: In media containing glucose, the combination of transcriptional shut-off and accelerated protein degradation yield rapid depletion of the RRF protein: 10 min after the media switch, RRF levels are visibly reduced in immunoblots; 15 min following a second transfer to fresh media containing glucose, the protein is nearly undetectable (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Bulk translation drops to about 40% by 5 min after the second transfer to glucose media and then levels off.
source: We observe that bulk translation drops to about 40% by the first time point and then levels off (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by HPG incorporation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the 60 min time point after RRF depletion, there is still a substantial amount of protein synthesis.
source: Even at the 60 min time point, there is still a substantial amount of protein synthesis.
evidence: Supported by HPG incorporation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ribosome profiling and RNA-seq were performed on the wild-type and RRF knockdown strains over an extended time course (5, 15, and 60 min) after the second media switch.
source: Using this strategy, we performed ribosome profiling and RNA-seq on the wild-type (WT) and RRF knockdown (KD) strains over an extended time course (5, 15, and 60 min) after the second media switch (Figure 1C).
evidence: Described in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Libraries were prepared from the same biological samples with a high-salt lysis buffer containing 1 M NaCl.
source: In addition to the standard ribosome profiling libraries, we also prepared libraries from the same biological samples with a high-salt lysis buffer containing 1 M NaCl.
evidence: Described in the methods.

claim: High-salt conditions dissociate ribosomes into 30S and 50S subunits unless the ribosomes are stabilized by the presence of an intact peptidyl-tRNA.
source: High-salt conditions are known to dissociate ribosomes into 30S and 50S subunits unless the ribosomes are stabilized by the presence of an intact peptidyl-tRNA (Zylber and Penman, 1970).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The loss of RRF increases the number of post-termination 70S complexes (post-TCs).
source: We anticipated that the loss of RRF would increase the number of post-termination 70S complexes (post-TCs).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known function of RRF.

claim: After 60 min of RRF depletion, there is a clear accumulation of RPFs in the 3′-UTR of the rpsB gene.
source: For example, although in the WT strain ribosome protected footprints (RPFs) from the rpsB gene map almost exclusively to the coding sequence, after 60 min of RRF depletion, there is a clear accumulation of RPFs in the 3′-UTR (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Even after only 5 min of RRF depletion, ribosome density is higher in the 3′-UTR in the KD strain than it is in the WT strain.
source: Even after only 5 min of RRF depletion, ribosome density is higher in the 3′-UTR in the KD strain than it is in the WT strain (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of RPFs in the 3′-UTR is even higher after 15 min or 60 min of RRF depletion.
source: The number of RPFs in the 3′-UTR is even higher after 15 min or 60 min of RRF depletion (Figure 2C&D).
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: The ribosome profiling protocol involves the isolation of 70S monosomes on a sucrose gradient after digestion of unprotected mRNA by nucleases.
source: Because the ribosome profiling protocol involves the isolation of 70S monosomes on a sucrose gradient after digestion of unprotected mRNA by nucleases, we are confident that these represent 70S ribosomes and not 30S subunits.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: 70S ribosomes accumulate significantly in the 3′-UTR when recycling fails.
source: These data show that 70S ribosomes accumulate significantly in the 3′-UTR when recycling fails but cannot distinguish between actively translating ribosomes and post-termination complexes (post-TCs).
evidence: Inferred from ribosome profiling data showing 3′-UTR accumulation.

claim: The distance from the stop codon to the first upstream peak of stacked ribosomes is about 25–30 nt, consistent with the footprint of a single ribosome.
source: The distance from the stop codon to the first upstream peak is about 25–30 nt, consistent with the footprint of a single ribosome, and a second peak is observed upstream at the distance of another footprint (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figures 2B-D.

claim: A second peak of stacked ribosomes is observed upstream at the distance of another footprint.
source: The distance from the stop codon to the first upstream peak is about 25–30 nt, consistent with the footprint of a single ribosome, and a second peak is observed upstream at the distance of another footprint (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figures 2B-D.

claim: The density corresponding to stacked ribosomes is more highly resolved in the ribosome profiling data collected using the high salt lysis buffer.
source: The density corresponding to these stacked ribosomes is more highly resolved in the ribosome profiling data collected using the high salt lysis buffer (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figures 2F-H.

claim: Ribosomes stably bound at the stop codon prevent elongating ribosomes from reaching the end of the ORF.
source: These data show that ribosomes stably bound at the stop codon prevent elongating ribosomes from reaching the end of the ORF as observed in S. cerevisiae upon depletion of Rli1 (Young et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from ribosome profiling data showing stacked ribosomes, with comparison to prior research in yeast.

claim: RRF plays a critical role in clearing post-termination complexes in vivo.
source: Taken together, our data show that RRF plays a critical role in clearing post-termination complexes in vivo, consistent with earlier in vitro biochemical studies.
evidence: Inferred from ribosome profiling data showing accumulation of post-TCs upon RRF depletion.

claim: The stop codon peak usually observed in standard RP experiments is lost in the high-salt samples.
source: Indeed, we see that the stop codon peak usually observed in standard RP experiments is lost in the high-salt samples, suggesting that this peak corresponds to post-TCs that are waiting for ribosome recycling.
evidence: Supported by comparison of standard and high-salt ribosome profiling data in Figure 2.

claim: The stop codon peak corresponds to post-TCs that are waiting for ribosome recycling.
source: Indeed, we see that the stop codon peak usually observed in standard RP experiments is lost in the high-salt samples, suggesting that this peak corresponds to post-TCs that are waiting for ribosome recycling.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the stop codon peak is lost in high-salt conditions.

claim: Post-TCs accumulate to high levels at stop codons.
source: The fact that post-TCs accumulate to high levels at stop codons argues that ribosome recycling is slower than peptidyl-hydrolysis even in wild-type cells, consistent with earlier observations in S. cerevisiae (Schuller et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from ribosome profiling data showing stop codon peaks.

claim: Ribosome recycling is slower than peptidyl-hydrolysis even in wild-type cells.
source: The fact that post-TCs accumulate to high levels at stop codons argues that ribosome recycling is slower than peptidyl-hydrolysis even in wild-type cells, consistent with earlier observations in S. cerevisiae (Schuller et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the accumulation of post-TCs at stop codons, with citation to prior research.

claim: A reduction in the 3′-UTR ribosome density is observed in the high-salt RP samples compared with the standard RP samples.
source: In addition, we observe a reduction in the 3′-UTR ribosome density in the high-salt RP samples compared with the standard RP samples (compare Figure 2B–D with Figure 2F–H).
evidence: Supported by comparison of ribosome profiling data in Figures 2B-D and 2F-H.

claim: For the 5 min time point, the high-salt wash reduces 3′-UTR density by 2.5-fold (p-value from one-sided Mann-Whitney test, 1.1 × 10−30).
source: For the 5 min time point, for example, the high-salt wash reduces 3′-UTR density by 2.5-fold (p-value from one-sided Mann-Whitney test, 1.1 × 10−30).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Most 3′-UTR ribosomes are not translating but have moved into the 3′-UTR by diffusion.
source: Again, the fact that 3′-UTR ribosomes are reduced by the high-salt lysis buffer argues that most of them are not translating but have moved into the 3′-UTR by diffusion.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that 3′-UTR ribosomes are reduced by high-salt treatment.

claim: The peaks corresponding to stacked ribosomes are not reduced by the high-salt conditions.
source: In contrast, the peaks corresponding to stacked ribosomes are not reduced by the high-salt conditions consistent with the idea that they represent elongating ribosomes whose intact peptidyl-tRNA stabilizes the subunits against dissociation in high salt.
evidence: Supported by comparison of standard and high-salt ribosome profiling data in Figure 2.

claim: Stacked ribosomes represent elongating ribosomes whose intact peptidyl-tRNA stabilizes the subunits against dissociation in high salt.
source: In contrast, the peaks corresponding to stacked ribosomes are not reduced by the high-salt conditions consistent with the idea that they represent elongating ribosomes whose intact peptidyl-tRNA stabilizes the subunits against dissociation in high salt.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that stacked ribosomes are not reduced by high-salt treatment.

claim: Reporters were designed for two genes (arcA and stpA) that show high levels of ribosome density in the 3′-UTR when RRF is depleted.
source: To directly test this possibility, we designed reporters for two genes (arcA and stpA) that show high levels of ribosome density in the 3′-UTR when RRF is depleted.
evidence: Described in the methods and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The GFP coding sequence was inserted into the 3′-UTR upstream of the first stop codon in every frame, creating three reporters, each in a different reading frame with respect to the upstream ORF.
source: To detect re-initiation events, we inserted the GFP coding sequence into the 3′-UTR upstream of the first stop codon in every frame, creating three reporters, each in a different reading frame with respect to the upstream ORF (in-frame, +1 or −1) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Described in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Little to no GFP was observed in the RRF+ condition for reporters with GFP in any of the three frames.
source: Little to no GFP was observed in the RRF+ condition for reporters with GFP in any of the three frames, suggesting that there are normally very low levels of initiation at the site where we inserted GFP into the 3′-UTR.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Upon RRF knockdown, no relative increase in GFP expression can be detected from the 3′-UTR in any reading frame for the arcA reporter.
source: Upon RRF knockdown, even though GFP levels are higher from the GFP-alone construct relative to the CysRS loading control (perhaps indicative of an increase in RNA levels), no relative increase in GFP expression can be detected from the 3′-UTR in any reading frame.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Re-initiation does not occur at high levels upon RRF depletion.
source: These data indicate that re-initiation does not occur at high levels upon RRF depletion.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of GFP expression from 3′-UTR reporters upon RRF depletion.

claim: For the stpA reporter, there was no increase in GFP expression in any of the reading frames upon RRF depletion.
source: Likewise, for the series of reporters based on stpA, there was no increase in GFP expression in any of the reading frames upon RRF depletion.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Re-initiation in the 3′-UTR is not a common event when RRF is depleted.
source: Together with the observation that much of the 3′-UTR ribosome density is lost upon high-salt treatment, these findings argue that re-initiation in the 3′-UTR is not a common event when RRF is depleted.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of GFP expression from 3′-UTR reporters and the high-salt sensitivity of 3′-UTR ribosomes.

claim: The number of stacked ribosomes would be particularly high on messages with high ribosome density.
source: We hypothesized that the number of stacked ribosomes would be particularly high on messages with high ribosome density.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the mechanism of ribosome stacking.

claim: High RO genes have significantly more stacked ribosomes, even at 5 min, with peaks corresponding to three or even four stacked ribosomes behind the post-TC complex at the stop codon.
source: As anticipated, the high RO genes have significantly more stacked ribosomes, even at 5 min, with peaks corresponding to three or even four stacked ribosomes behind the post-TC complex at the stop codon.
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For all three RRF KD samples (5, 15, and 60 min of depletion), the collision scores are higher for high RO genes than for low RO genes.
source: We observe that for all three RRF KD samples (5, 15, and 60 min of depletion), the collision scores are higher for high RO genes than for low RO genes (Figure 4B, p-values from one-sided Mann-Whitney tests: 7.6 × 10−23, 6.6 × 10−16, 5.4 × 10−15, respectively).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Highly translated genes have more ribosomes per mRNA, increasing the chance for collisions of elongating ribosomes with post-TCs trapped at stop codons.
source: These data show that because highly translated genes have more ribosomes per mRNA, there is an increased chance for collisions of elongating ribosomes with post-TCs trapped at stop codons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that high RO genes have higher collision scores.

claim: Genes with high RO have fewer ribosome footprints in the 3′-UTR relative to the CDS than genes with low RO.
source: Unexpectedly, genes with high RO have fewer ribosome footprints in the 3′-UTR relative to the CDS than genes with low RO (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At each time point, the 3′-UTR scores are lower in high RO genes than in low RO genes.
source: At each time point, the 3′-UTR scores are lower in high RO genes than in low RO genes (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The stacking of ribosomes that occurs in high RO genes might stabilize post-TCs at the stop codon.
source: One possible explanation is that the stacking of ribosomes that occurs in high RO genes might stabilize post-TCs at the stop codon.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation that high RO genes have lower 3′-UTR scores.

claim: Ribosome collisions result in stable disome structures with extensive contacts between the 40S subunits in eukaryotes.
source: In eukaryotes, ribosome collisions result in stable disome structures with extensive contacts between the 40S subunits (Juszkiewicz et al., 2018; Ikeuchi et al., 2019); similar interactions have also been observed in structures of bacterial polysomes (Brandt et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Similar ribosome-ribosome interactions have been observed in structures of bacterial polysomes.
source: In eukaryotes, ribosome collisions result in stable disome structures with extensive contacts between the 40S subunits (Juszkiewicz et al., 2018; Ikeuchi et al., 2019); similar interactions have also been observed in structures of bacterial polysomes (Brandt et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Ribosome-ribosome interactions or the binding of associated factors may prevent post-TCs in high RO genes from diffusing into the 3′-UTR.
source: Here, ribosome-ribosome interactions or the binding of associated factors may prevent post-TCs in high RO genes from diffusing into the 3′-UTR.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation that high RO genes have lower 3′-UTR scores.

claim: Many genes in bacterial genomes are organized in polycistronic operons.
source: One of the distinctive characteristics of bacterial genomes is that many genes are organized in polycistronic operons.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: For translationally coupled genes, translation of a downstream gene in an operon is dependent on the translation of an upstream gene.
source: For translationally coupled genes, translation of a downstream gene in an operon is dependent on the translation of an upstream gene (Oppenheim and Yanofsky, 1980).
evidence: This is a definition based on established scientific knowledge, with citation.

claim: Without RRF and ribosome recycling, the number of scanning 30S subunits should be markedly reduced.
source: Without RRF and ribosome recycling, the number of scanning 30S subunits should be markedly reduced.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the proposed mechanism of translational coupling.

claim: Five gene pairs were selected that have been directly demonstrated to exhibit translational coupling: trpB-trpA, galT-galK, prfA-prmC, rpmI-rplT, and rplK-rplA.
source: These gene pairs are: trpB-trpA (Aksoy et al., 1984), galT-galK (Schümperli et al., 1982), prfA-prmC (Heurgué-Hamard et al., 2002), rpmI-rplT (Chiaruttini et al., 1996), and rplK-rplA (Baughman and Nomura, 1983; Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Translational coupling was observed for all five reporter constructs.
source: As expected, we observe translational coupling for all five reporter constructs: nLuc was expressed more strongly from the RBS reporter than from the NoRBS reporter in each case.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The ratio of the nLuc/fLuc values for the RBS reporter and the NoRBS reporter reveals the degree of translational coupling.
source: The ratio of the nLuc/fLuc values for the RBS reporter and the NoRBS reporter reveals the degree of translational coupling.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The coupling ratios ranged for the five gene pairs from 1.7 for trpB-trpA to 7.0 for rplK-rplA.
source: These ratios ranged for the five gene pairs from 1.7 for trpB-trpA to 7.0 for rplK-rplA (Figure 5C), validating that this assay measures translational coupling as designed.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The level of translational coupling did not change significantly upon RRF depletion.
source: Importantly, the level of translational coupling did not change significantly upon RRF depletion (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Even after 60 min of RRF depletion, where significant ribosome density accumulates in the untranslated region between the clpP and clpX genes, there are no discernable effects on the translation of the downstream clpX gene.
source: As shown for the clpPX operon in Figure 6A, even after 60 min of RRF depletion, where significant ribosome density accumulates in the untranslated region between the clpP and clpX genes, there are no discernable effects on the translation of the downstream clpX gene; the ratio of ribosome density (clpP/clpX) is very close to one both before and after RRF depletion.
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is a strong correlation (r = 0.89) between the ratio of ribosome density for the upstream and downstream genes between the RRF KD and the WT strains.
source: There is a strong correlation (r = 0.89) between the ratio of ribosome density for the upstream and downstream genes between the RRF KD and the WT strains, indicating that the loss of RRF does not dramatically dysregulate the expression of the downstream genes across the transcriptome.
evidence: Supported by genome-wide analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The loss of RRF does not dramatically dysregulate the expression of the downstream genes across the transcriptome.
source: There is a strong correlation (r = 0.89) between the ratio of ribosome density for the upstream and downstream genes between the RRF KD and the WT strains, indicating that the loss of RRF does not dramatically dysregulate the expression of the downstream genes across the transcriptome.
evidence: Inferred from the strong correlation observed in the genome-wide analysis.

claim: Generally, the longer the distance between coupled genes, the lower the efficiency of coupling.
source: One such feature is the distance between the coupled ORFs: generally, the longer the distance between the genes, the lower the efficiency of coupling (Levin-Karp et al., 2013; Tian and Salis, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The two groups of gene pairs (twofold increased vs. twofold decreased upon RRF depletion) have distributions of intergenic lengths that are not significantly different statistically (p-value from one-sided Mann-Whitney test, 0.36).
source: We compared the intergenic regions in the gene pairs whose ratios are twofold increased upon RRF depletion to those gene pairs that are twofold decreased; the two groups have distributions of intergenic lengths (Figure 6C) that are not significantly different statistically (p-value from one-sided Mann-Whitney test, 0.36).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In E. coli, more than 30% of gene pairs have overlapping stop and start sites.
source: In E. coli, more than 30% of gene pairs have overlapping stop and start sites.
evidence: This is a statement about genome organization in E. coli.

claim: For gene pairs with overlapping stop and start codons, the WT and RRF-depleted strains are highly correlated.
source: We plotted the ratio of upstream and downstream ribosome density for these pairs and again observed that the WT and RRF-depleted strains are highly correlated (Figure 6D), arguing against the possibility that RRF plays a special role in these overlapping intergenic regions.
evidence: Supported by genome-wide analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Loss of ribosome recycling does not have a dramatic effect on translational coupling at the genome-wide level.
source: Collectively, these data show that loss of ribosome recycling does not have a dramatic effect on translational coupling at the genome-wide level.
evidence: Inferred from the genome-wide analyses showing high correlation between WT and RRF KD strains.

claim: After 60 min of RRF depletion, the number of ribosome footprints on 16 genes were more than 10-fold higher in the RRF KD strain than in the WT strain.
source: After 60 min of RRF depletion, we found that the number of ribosome footprints on 16 genes were more than 10-fold higher in the RRF KD strain than in the WT strain, indicating higher levels of protein synthesis (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: One of the most prominent changes in gene expression upon RRF depletion is in the expression of the ArfA protein (39-fold).
source: One of the most prominent changes is in the expression of the ArfA protein (39-fold), a factor known to rescue stalled ribosomes (Chadani et al., 2010; Chadani et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: ArfA is a factor known to rescue stalled ribosomes.
source: One of the most prominent changes is in the expression of the ArfA protein (39-fold), a factor known to rescue stalled ribosomes (Chadani et al., 2010; Chadani et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A small increase in the levels of synthesis of ArfA protein was observed after 15 min of RRF depletion.
source: Although we observed a small increase in the levels of synthesis of ArfA protein after 15 min, the full 39-fold induction was observed after 60 min (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Changes in ArfA protein synthesis levels were accompanied by a corresponding up-regulation of the steady state levels of arfA mRNA.
source: These changes in protein synthesis levels were accompanied by a corresponding up-regulation of the steady state levels of arfA mRNA (Figure 7C), arguing that the regulation acts at the RNA level.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The regulation of ArfA acts at the RNA level.
source: These changes in protein synthesis levels were accompanied by a corresponding up-regulation of the steady state levels of arfA mRNA (Figure 7C), arguing that the regulation acts at the RNA level.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both mRNA and protein levels increase.

claim: Expression of nLuc from the arfA promoter did not change significantly upon RRF depletion.
source: Importantly, expression of nLuc from the arfA promoter did not change significantly upon RRF depletion, arguing against a strong induction of transcription and leading us to look for other explanations for the dramatic increase in the steady-state level of arfA mRNA.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The increase in arfA mRNA levels cannot be explained by higher levels of transcription.
source: Importantly, expression of nLuc from the arfA promoter did not change significantly upon RRF depletion, arguing against a strong induction of transcription and leading us to look for other explanations for the dramatic increase in the steady-state level of arfA mRNA.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of change in promoter activity upon RRF depletion.

claim: The expression of arfA is regulated post-transcriptionally based on the demand for ribosome rescue activity in the cell.
source: The expression of arfA is regulated post-transcriptionally based on the demand for ribosome rescue activity in the cell (Garza-Sánchez et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: arfA mRNA contains a hairpin structure that is constitutively cleaved by RNase III leading to the production of a processed mRNA lacking a stop codon.
source: arfA mRNA contains a hairpin structure that is constitutively cleaved by RNase III leading to the production of a processed mRNA lacking a stop codon (a 'non-stop' mRNA).
evidence: This is established knowledge about arfA regulation.

claim: Ribosome stalling at the 3′-end of the truncated arfA transcript is resolved by tmRNA, which tags the truncated ArfA protein to target it for degradation.
source: Ribosome stalling at the 3′-end of this truncated arfA transcript is resolved by the primary ribosome rescue factor, tmRNA, which tags the truncated ArfA protein to target it for degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about arfA regulation.

claim: tmRNA recruits RNase R so that the arfA mRNA is rapidly degraded.
source: tmRNA also recruits RNase R so that the arfA mRNA is rapidly degraded (Richards et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: If tmRNA is overwhelmed or inactive, ArfA expression increases and together with RF2 provides a backup mechanism to rescue stalled ribosomes.
source: If tmRNA is overwhelmed or inactive, ArfA expression increases and together with RF2 provides a backup mechanism to rescue stalled ribosomes (Chadani et al., 2010; Chadani et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The increase in arfA mRNA levels is explained by inhibition of tmRNA activity and reduced rates of mRNA decay by RNase R.
source: Based on this, we suspected that the increase in arfA mRNA levels that we observe is explained by inhibition of tmRNA activity and reduced rates of mRNA decay by RNase R.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known regulation of arfA.

claim: After only 5 min of RRF depletion, there is a sharp increase in ribosome footprints on the short ORF within tmRNA.
source: After only 5 min of RRF depletion, we see a sharp increase in ribosome footprints on the short ORF within tmRNA (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The strongest peak of ribosome footprints on tmRNA is at the stop codon, suggesting an accumulation of post-TCs that cannot be recycled.
source: The strongest peak is at the stop codon, suggesting an accumulation of post-TCs that cannot be recycled.
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: 60 min after depletion of RRF, there is an accumulation of ribosome footprints downstream of the tmRNA ORF, in regions that are normally not translated but play important structural roles.
source: 60 min after depletion of RRF, we also see an accumulation of ribosome footprints downstream of the tmRNA ORF, in regions that are normally not translated but play important structural roles.
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The downstream footprints on tmRNA are reminiscent of the accumulated 3′-UTR ribosomes in all mRNAs and likely represent non-translating 70S ribosomes.
source: These downstream footprints are reminiscent of the accumulated 3′-UTR ribosomes in all mRNAs and likely represent non-translating 70S ribosomes; consistent with this explanation, there is less ribosome density in tmRNA in the high-salt treated samples where post-TCs are destabilized (data not shown).
evidence: Inferred from comparison with 3′-UTR ribosomes and high-salt sensitivity.

claim: Post-TCs on tmRNA denature key structures in tmRNA, interfering with its ability to rescue stalled ribosomes.
source: We speculate that these post-TCs denature key structures in tmRNA, interfering with its ability to rescue stalled ribosomes and thus preventing it from promoting degradation of ArfA at the mRNA and protein levels.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed effects on tmRNA and ArfA.

claim: Post-TCs on tmRNA prevent it from promoting degradation of ArfA at the mRNA and protein levels.
source: We speculate that these post-TCs denature key structures in tmRNA, interfering with its ability to rescue stalled ribosomes and thus preventing it from promoting degradation of ArfA at the mRNA and protein levels.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed effects on tmRNA and ArfA.

claim: A translation-based feedback pathway which responds to aberrant cellular translation is induced by the loss of ribosome recycling.
source: These findings reveal how a translation-based feedback pathway which responds to aberrant cellular translation is induced by the loss of ribosome recycling.
evidence: Inferred from the observed effects on tmRNA and ArfA upon RRF depletion.

claim: The approach to deplete RRF probably does not lead to total loss of this essential factor; low levels of recycling likely occur in RRF-depleted cells.
source: First, our approach probably does not lead to total loss of this essential factor; low levels of recycling likely occur in RRF-depleted cells.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: RRF depletion may lead to indirect effects on biological pathways unrelated to recycling.
source: A second caveat is that RRF depletion may lead to indirect effects. Biological pathways unrelated to recycling may be impacted when the translation of critical proteins is reduced.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: Most of the phenotypes of RRF depletion occur even at the earliest time point (5 min), where indirect effects are most unlikely.
source: In addition, most of the phenotypes of RRF depletion described here occur even at the earliest time point (5 min), where indirect effects are most unlikely.
evidence: This is an argument against the significance of indirect effects.

claim: Post-TCs retain some affinity for the site where termination occurred due to base-pairing between the deacyl-tRNA in the P-site and the last sense codon in the ORF.
source: We speculate that post-TCs retain some affinity for the site where termination occurred due to base-pairing between the deacyl-tRNA in the P-site and the last sense codon in the ORF.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed ribosome stacking.

claim: Over time, post-TCs, only weakly retained by codon-anticodon pairing with the tRNA, eventually slide along the mRNA past the stop codon into the 3′ UTR.
source: We argue that over time, post-TCs, only weakly retained by codon-anticodon pairing with the tRNA, eventually slide along the mRNA past the stop codon into the 3′ UTR.
evidence: This is an explanation for the accumulation of ribosomes in the 3′-UTR.

claim: The dramatic enrichment of ribosome density downstream of stop codons highlights the importance of RRF in maintaining ribosome homeostasis by regenerating ribosome subunits to initiate translation.
source: The dramatic enrichment of ribosome density downstream of stop codons highlights the importance of RRF in maintaining ribosome homeostasis by regenerating ribosome subunits to initiate translation.
evidence: Inferred from the observed accumulation of ribosomes in the 3′-UTR upon RRF depletion.

claim: When RRF is depleted, many ribosomes are trapped in an inactive state in the 3′-UTR.
source: When RRF is depleted, many ribosomes are trapped in an inactive state in the 3′-UTR, as seen in earlier studies (Guydosh and Green, 2014; Mills et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from ribosome profiling data, with citations to prior research.

claim: The Dom34/Hbs1 complex delivers Dom34 to the ribosomal A site in eukaryotes, where it works together with Rli1 to promote subunit splitting.
source: The Dom34/Hbs1 complex (normally involved in rescuing stalled ribosomes) delivers Dom34 to the ribosomal A site, where it works together with the canonical recycling factor Rli1 to promote subunit splitting (Shoemaker and Green, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Loss of Dom34 in S. cerevisiae leads to the accumulation of non-translating ribosomes in the 3′-UTR.
source: In S. cerevisiae, loss of Dom34 leads to the accumulation of non-translating ribosomes in the 3′-UTR, indicating that Dom34 normally helps remove empty 80S ribosomes from 3′-UTRs (Guydosh and Green, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The Dom34/Rli1 complex can serve as a backup mechanism to recycle post-TCs that have escaped canonical recycling at the stop codon by eRF1/Rli1.
source: Because the Dom34/Rli1 complex directly splits ribosomal subunits whether there is an intact peptidyl-tRNA linkage or not, it can serve as a backup mechanism to recycle post-TCs that have escaped canonical recycling at the stop codon by eRF1/Rli1 (Young et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the properties of the Dom34/Rli1 complex, with citation to prior research.

claim: The bacterial tmRNA/SmpB and ArfA/RF2 ribosome rescue systems typically catalyze reactions with the peptidyl-tRNA.
source: In contrast, the bacterial tmRNA/SmpB and ArfA/RF2 ribosome rescue systems typically catalyze reactions with the peptidyl-tRNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial ribosome rescue systems.

claim: Bacteria may lack an effective backup mechanism for splitting post-TCs.
source: It may be that bacteria lack an effective backup mechanism for splitting post-TCs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences between bacteria and eukaryotes.

claim: The critical role that RRF plays in ribosome homeostasis likely is the simplest explanation for its essential nature.
source: The critical role that RRF plays in ribosome homeostasis likely is the simplest explanation for its essential nature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed importance of RRF in ribosome recycling.

claim: In yeast, ribosome density in the 3′-UTR upon knockdown of Rli1 or 40S recycling factors at least in part reflects the activity of elongating ribosomes.
source: In yeast, ribosome density in the 3′-UTR upon knockdown of Rli1 or 40S recycling factors at least in part reflects the activity of elongating ribosomes (Young et al., 2015; Young et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Translation in the 3′-UTR in yeast arises from re-initiation downstream of the stop codon.
source: Although the mechanism is poorly understood, translation in the 3′-UTR does arise from re-initiation downstream of the stop codon.
evidence: This is a statement about yeast based on prior research.

claim: The 3′-UTR ribosome density in E. coli reflects post-TCs that are not translating.
source: In contrast, the 3′-UTR ribosome density in E. coli reflects post-TCs that are not translating, as evidenced by their sensitivity to the high-salt buffer (Figure 2) and our failure to detect an increase in translation of GFP in the 3′-UTR when RRF is depleted (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by high-salt ribosome profiling data (Figure 2) and GFP reporter assays (Figure 3).

claim: Eukaryotic ribosomes scan from the 5′-end of mRNAs to find start codons.
source: In general, eukaryotic ribosomes scan from the 5′-end of mRNAs to find start codons (Hinnebusch, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Short, upstream ORFs play an important role in regulating translation in eukaryotes.
source: Given the importance of short, upstream ORFs in regulating translation in eukaryotes, ribosomes must be able to re-initiate following termination (Gunišová et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Ribosomes must be able to re-initiate following termination in eukaryotes.
source: Given the importance of short, upstream ORFs in regulating translation in eukaryotes, ribosomes must be able to re-initiate following termination (Gunišová et al., 2018).
evidence: Inferred from the importance of upstream ORFs, with citation to prior research.

claim: Bacterial 30S subunits normally initiate anywhere along a polycistronic mRNA where they are recruited directly based on sequence context and mRNA structure.
source: On the other hand, bacterial 30S subunits normally initiate anywhere along a polycistronic mRNA where they are recruited directly based on sequence context and mRNA structure (Salis et al., 2009; Del Campo et al., 2015; Burkhardt et al., 2017; Baez et al., 2019; Saito et al., 2020), without the need for scanning.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Bacterial 30S subunits initiate translation without the need for scanning.
source: On the other hand, bacterial 30S subunits normally initiate anywhere along a polycistronic mRNA where they are recruited directly based on sequence context and mRNA structure (Salis et al., 2009; Del Campo et al., 2015; Burkhardt et al., 2017; Baez et al., 2019; Saito et al., 2020), without the need for scanning.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: One common mechanistic model of translational coupling argues that following termination and subunit splitting, the 30S subunit remains on the mRNA and slides until it re-initiates at a nearby start codon.
source: One common mechanistic model argues that following termination and subunit splitting, the 30S subunit remains on the mRNA and slides until it re-initiates at a nearby start codon (Adhin and van Duin, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Initiation by 70S ribosomes is difficult to reconcile with the well-characterized biochemical activities of fMet-tRNA and initiation factors that initiate translation on 30S subunits.
source: We note that initiation by 70S ribosomes is difficult to reconcile with the well-characterized biochemical activities of fMet-tRNA and initiation factors that initiate translation on 30S subunits (Simonetti et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an argument based on established biochemical knowledge, with citation.

claim: The loss of RRF does not affect the relative translational levels of neighboring genes in polycistronic messages.
source: Contrary to the predictions of both of these models, however, we observed that the loss of RRF does not affect the relative translational levels of neighboring genes in polycistronic messages.
evidence: Supported by reporter assays and genome-wide ribosome profiling analyses.

claim: Re-initiation is not the dominant mechanism for translational coupling in E. coli.
source: We conclude that re-initiation is not the dominant mechanism for translational coupling in E. coli, although we cannot rule out the possibility that it may occur in specific contexts.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of RRF depletion on translational coupling.

claim: The data are most consistent with models of de novo initiation, where free 30S subunits are recruited to start codons directly.
source: Instead, our data are most consistent with models of de novo initiation, where free 30S subunits are recruited to start codons directly.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of RRF depletion on translational coupling.

claim: In cases where neighboring genes are translationally coupled, it seems likely that melting of mRNA structure near the downstream start site is the mechanism at play.
source: In cases where neighboring genes are translationally coupled, it seems likely that melting of mRNA structure near the downstream start site is the mechanism at play.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed data and prior research.

claim: The melting of mRNA structures is a well-documented mechanism for coupling the translation of neighboring genes.
source: The melting of mRNA structures is a well-documented mechanism for coupling the translation of neighboring genes where it has been explored in detail (Rex et al., 1994; Chiaruttini et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several genome-wide studies of mRNA structure and translation argued that mRNA structure is a major determinant of translational efficiency in bacteria.
source: Moreover, several genome-wide studies of mRNA structure and translation argued that mRNA structure is a major determinant of translational efficiency in bacteria (Del Campo et al., 2015; Burkhardt et al., 2017; Mustoe et al., 2018), perhaps even more important than well-studied sequence elements such as Shine-Dalgarno motifs (Saito et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: mRNA structure may be even more important than Shine-Dalgarno motifs in determining translational efficiency in bacteria.
source: Moreover, several genome-wide studies of mRNA structure and translation argued that mRNA structure is a major determinant of translational efficiency in bacteria (Del Campo et al., 2015; Burkhardt et al., 2017; Mustoe et al., 2018), perhaps even more important than well-studied sequence elements such as Shine-Dalgarno motifs (Saito et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.
